sections.title: Overview
blocks: This is a group of reactions in which a drug causes vesicles, bullae, pustules or epidermal necrosis. They range from trivial (localised FDE) to life-threatening (TEN). For the IP, **drug causation** is the main reason to know them.

**SJS and TEN** are one disease spectrum. They are rare, life-threatening **mucocutaneous** reactions, almost always drug-induced, with widespread **keratinocyte death and epidermal detachment**. They are classified by the **maximum % BSA detached** (Bastuji-Garin):
Incidence is ~1–6 per million per year (higher in HIV). Mortality is ~**5–10% for SJS** and **~30% (25–50%) for TEN**; it is higher in older people and those with comorbidity.

**Erythema multiforme (EM)** is a *different* disease. It is usually triggered by **HSV** (or *Mycoplasma*), and drugs cause it only rarely. It gives **typical raised 3-zone target lesions on the acral skin**, with or without mild mucosal involvement ("EM major"), and has a good prognosis (see the [inflammatory rash pages](condition:erythema-multiforme) notes).

ul: **High-risk ("notorious") drugs** (EuroSCAR/RegiSCAR, BAD 2016): **allopurinol** (the commonest in Europe), **carbamazepine**, **lamotrigine** (especially fast titration or co-prescribed with **valproate**), **phenytoin**, **phenobarbital**, **sulfonamides** (co-trimoxazole, sulfasalazine), **oxicam NSAIDs** (meloxicam, piroxicam), **nevirapine**. Lower risk: other antibiotics (aminopenicillins, cephalosporins, quinolones), paracetamol (controversial), PPIs. ~5–15% of cases are idiopathic or *Mycoplasma*-related (especially in children).

**Latency:** typically **4–28 days** after the first dose (BAD 2016; ALDEN "suggestive" window **5–28 days**). It is shorter on re-exposure (hours to 2 days). Drugs used for many months are rarely culprits, and anticonvulsants mostly cause it within the first 8 weeks.

sections.title: Clinical features
blocks: **SJS/TEN** classification by detached BSA: **SJS <10%**, **SJS/TEN overlap 10–30%**, **TEN >30%** (**Module 4 exam Q27**, 40% = TEN).

ul: Prodrome: fever, sore throat and eye symptoms 1–3 days before the skin.
Then **painful** dusky macules or atypical flat targets, which form bullae and sheet-like detachment with a positive Nikolsky sign.
**≥2 mucosal sites** are involved (oral haemorrhagic crusting of the lips, conjunctivitis, genital; photo E02).

blocks: **SSSS** is the toxin-mediated mimic in young children: superficial peeling, mucosa **spared**, and the child is irritable and tender.

ul: **Prodrome (1–3 days):** fever, malaise, sore throat, conjunctivitis/photophobia, painful swallowing — often treated as an infection, which leads to new drugs (NSAIDs, antibiotics) that confuse the timeline.

**Skin:** **painful** dusky-red macules and **atypical flat targets** (two zones, purpuric centres) on the trunk and face, spreading and coalescing. Flaccid blisters and **sheet-like detachment** follow ("wet cigarette paper"); **Nikolsky positive**.
**Mucosae (≥2 sites in >90%):** haemorrhagic crusted lips, oral erosions, conjunctivitis/pseudomembranes, genital and urethral erosions; also respiratory/GI epithelium.

**Systemic:** fever, tachycardia, fluid and protein loss, hypothermia, sepsis (skin barrier lost), acute kidney injury, hepatitis (raised ALT), anaemia, **lymphopenia** (common), neutropenia (poor prognosis), and respiratory involvement (bronchial sloughing).

**Sequelae** (in up to 50–90% of survivors): **ocular** dry eye, trichiasis, **symblepharon** and corneal scarring/blindness; pigmentary change; **nail loss/dystrophy**; scarring; genital adhesions; oesophageal/urethral strictures; psychological trauma.

blocks: Diagnosis is mostly clinical, with urgent specialist confirmation and frozen-section or standard biopsy. **SCORTEN** (calculated in the first 24 h) predicts mortality. Its 7 points are:
For drug causation use **ALDEN** (for SJS/TEN). Patch testing is useful later for FDE and AGEP. For DRESS (the systemic DDx), RegiSCAR.

ul: **Clinical diagnosis + urgent skin biopsy:** H&E shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis with sparse dermal infiltrate. Take a second sample for **direct immunofluorescence (negative)** to exclude autoimmune bullous disease.
**Severity at admission — SCORTEN** (calculate within 24 h, repeat on day 3), 1 point each:

blocks: (Bastuji-Garin et al., 2000. It is endorsed by BAD 2016 and tends to over-predict mortality in modern care; ABCD-10 is an alternative.)

ul: **Drug causality — ALDEN** (Algorithm of Drug causality for Epidermal Necrolysis; Sassolas et al., 2010). Score **every** drug taken in the 8 weeks before the **index day** (the first day of symptoms, including the prodrome):

rows: 1. **Delay** from first intake to index day
**5–28 days +3**; 29–56 days +2; 1–4 days +1; >56 days −1; **started on or after the index day −3** (previous reaction to the same drug: 1–4 days +3, 5–56 days +1)
2. **Drug present** in the body on the index day
Definite 0; doubtful −1; **excluded −3** (stopped >5 half-lives before the index day, with normal clearance)
SJS/TEN with same drug +4; similar drug or other reaction with the same drug +2; other reaction with a similar drug +1; no known exposure 0; **previous exposure without reaction −2**
**High-risk ("strongly associated") +3**; associated +2; suspected +1; unknown 0; not suspected −1
If any drug has an intermediate score >3, subtract 1 from each of the other drugs
**<0 very unlikely; 0–1 unlikely; 2–3 possible; 4–5 probable; ≥6 very probable**

sections.title: Management

ul: **Suspected SJS/TEN or extensive or mucosal blistering:** **STOP all non-essential drugs immediately**, especially the likely culprits started 4–28 days ago; **999 / same-day ED** for transfer to a **burns or dermatology intensive unit** (UK SJS/TEN guideline, Creamer 2016). Don't wait for a GP appointment; **Ophthalmology within 24 h**, and urology/gynaecology/oral medicine input; Specialist adjuncts: ciclosporin, IVIG (the evidence for blocking Fas-FasL is mixed and UK guidance does not routinely recommend it), steroids, and anti-TNF (etanercept, being studied)
**AGEP:** stop the drug, give supportive care and a potent TCS. Refer the same day if febrile or extensive.
**FDE:** stop and avoid the culprit; a potent TCS for 1–2 weeks; document the specific drug.
**Drug-induced BP or pemphigus:** stop the culprit and follow the specialist pathway. Recovery may take months.

**Allergy documentation:** Record the exact drug and reaction in the GP record (SNOMED) and on the patient's allergy list; **Report to MHRA Yellow Card** (all serious reactions; anything involving a black-triangle drug); For SJS/TEN: lifelong avoidance of the culprit and **structurally related drugs**, and **advice for first-degree relatives** about HLA risk. A MedicAlert bracelet is reasonable

**Prevention (pharmacist role):** **HLA-B*15:02** screening before carbamazepine in people of Han Chinese or Thai ancestry (BNF/MHRA); Start allopurinol low (100 mg) and titrate in CKD; Follow the **lamotrigine** titration schedule (halve doses with valproate), and counsel all new starters to **stop and seek help with any rash, fever or mouth ulcers in the first 8 weeks**

blocks: **Primary-care/community actions (you will see the prodrome or early rash):**

ol: **Suspect it:** a new drug in the past 8 weeks + skin pain + dusky/target lesions or blisters + **mucositis** + fever.
**Stop all suspect drugs immediately.** Delay in withdrawal raises mortality; early withdrawal of drugs with a short half-life improves survival (Garcia-Doval 2000).

**Same-day emergency admission** (999/ED with a call to on-call dermatology). The BAD advises transfer to a **specialist centre (burns unit/ITU or dermatology with specialist MDT)** when BSA >10% or the patient is unwell. Do **not** start oral steroids or antibiotics in primary care "to cover".

**Document** the culprit(s) prominently, **report via Yellow Card**, and tell the patient and family that the drug and **structurally related drugs** must be avoided for life (aromatic anticonvulsants carbamazepine/phenytoin/phenobarbital/oxcarbazepine/lamotrigine cross-react; avoid all sulfonamide antibiotics after co-trimoxazole SJS). Advise a **medical alert** bracelet/card.
**First-degree relatives** may share the HLA risk — mention this for carbamazepine/allopurinol.

ul: **Supportive care is the cornerstone:** warmed environment (25–28 °C); pressure-relieving/air-fluidised mattress; barrier nursing; fluids guided by urine output (avoid over-resuscitation); nutrition (NG feed); analgesia (incl. for dressing changes); VTE prophylaxis; stress-ulcer prophylaxis; repeated swabs, with **no prophylactic antibiotics**

**Skin:** leave detached epidermis in place as a biological dressing; decompress blisters; whole-body greasy emollient (e.g. 50% white soft paraffin/50% liquid paraffin); non-adherent silicone dressings.
**Eyes:** **ophthalmology review within 24 h** of admission, then daily. Lubricants, topical steroid/antibiotic drops, lysis of adhesions (amniotic membrane in severe disease).

**Mouth:** white soft paraffin to the lips, benzydamine/mucoprotectant mouthwashes, antiseptic chlorhexidine mouthwash, and a corticosteroid mouthwash (e.g. betamethasone soluble tablet in water) — doses per BAD/BNF.
**Urogenital:** review; catheter; potent topical steroid to non-eroded mucosa; dressings to prevent adhesions.

**Immunomodulation:** no treatment is proven (BAD 2016, Cochrane 2022). Options used in UK centres, decided by the specialist team: **ciclosporin** (~3 mg/kg/day for 7–10 days), which has the most observational support; IVIg; short pulsed corticosteroids early; **etanercept** (emerging RCT data)

blocks: Recognition, **stopping drugs, emergency referral, documentation and Yellow Card** are core IP responsibilities. All treatment is in secondary care. After discharge: lifelong avoidance list, eye follow-up, psychological support, and checks on all new prescriptions and OTC sales (e.g. no ibuprofen if an NSAID was implicated).

refer.t: **Skin pain, fever, dusky targets, mucosal erosions or skin detachment**: SJS/TEN, stop all non-essential drugs and call 999 / admit (burns unit or ICU).
Widespread sterile pustules with fever after a new drug (AGEP): same-day assessment.
Rash with fever, facial swelling, lymph nodes and abnormal liver tests: **DRESS**.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: **Skin pain, fever, dusky targets, mucosal erosions or skin detachment**: SJS/TEN, stop all non-essential drugs and call 999 / admit (burns unit or ICU).
Widespread sterile pustules with fever after a new drug (AGEP): same-day assessment.
Rash with fever, facial swelling, lymph nodes and abnormal liver tests: **DRESS**.

blocks: Any suspected SJS/TEN → **same-day admission**. Red flags: skin pain, ≥2 mucosal sites, dusky/atypical targets, Nikolsky sign, fever, conjunctivitis with rash, BSA detachment, dehydration, inability to eat/drink.

pearls: Ask **"What new medicine did you start in the last 8 weeks?"** at every acute rash with fever, skin pain or mucosal involvement.
**Skin pain out of proportion + mucosal erosions + dusky skin = SJS/TEN** until proven otherwise.
Paracetamol can cause FDE, so don't assume over-the-counter means innocent. Always ask about OTC and herbal products.
"**Pain out of proportion + mouth/eye involvement + a new drug = SJS until proven otherwise.**"
The prodrome is treated as an infection, so the drugs given for it (NSAIDs, antibiotics) appear on the chart just before the rash — **ALDEN's "started after index day −3"** stops you blaming them.

**Prevention at prescribing:** test for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in people of SE Asian ancestry. Start allopurinol low (≤100 mg, lower in CKD) and titrate. **Titrate lamotrigine exactly as in the SmPC** (halve the dose with valproate) and warn about rash in the first 8 weeks. Avoid co-trimoxazole where alternatives exist.
Patient leaflet: "If you develop a rash with blisters, sore mouth or sore eyes, stop the medicine and seek urgent help."
